chapter.name: Connecting the Dots
chapter.blurb: Statistical questions and statements, the arithmetic mean, comparing data with range and dot plots, the median and outliers, mean versus median, double bar graphs and reading data tables.

scope: Tell statistical questions and statistical statements from other questions and statements
Find the arithmetic mean (average) of data, understand it as a fair share, and compare groups of different sizes by their means
Describe and compare data using the minimum, maximum, range, total and mean, and read a dot plot
Find the median of data with an odd or even number of values and recognise outliers and their effect on the mean
Compare the mean and median, tell zero from no value, and choose which measure of central tendency represents the data
Read and draw clustered column (double bar) graphs, choose a scale, and interpret them in two steps
Read data tables and graphs to find patterns, compare groups over time, and decide which statements the data can justify
Mode and frequency tables -- not taught in this chapter
Pie charts and line graphs -- only dot plots and double bar graphs are used
Standard deviation and other formal measures of spread -- only range is used
The number lock puzzle and the individual and group projects -- activities that are not assessed

concepts.name: Statistical questions and statements
concepts.description: Telling a statistical question, one answered by collecting data that varies, from an ordinary question, and recognising statistical statements.
concepts.idea: A question whose answer varies from one person or time to another can only be answered by collecting data.
concepts.rule: A statistical question expects varied answers and is answered with data; a statistical statement summarises data with numbers, proportions or predictions.
concepts.example: How tall are the Grade 7 students in our school? is statistical; How tall is Meena? is not.

concepts.name: Arithmetic mean (average)
concepts.description: Finding the arithmetic mean of a list of values, understanding it as a fair share and comparing groups of different sizes by their means.
concepts.idea: The mean is the equal share each value would get if the total were shared out evenly, so it balances the highs and lows.
concepts.rule: Mean = sum of all the values divided by the number of values.
concepts.example: The guava counts 3, 8, 10, 5, 4 have total 30 and mean 30 / 5 = 6.

concepts.name: Comparing data with range, totals and dot plots
concepts.description: Describing and comparing data using the minimum, maximum, range, total and mean, and reading a dot plot.
concepts.idea: Different summaries answer different questions, and no single one gives the full picture of which group is better.
concepts.rule: Range = maximum - minimum; a dot plot shows every value as a dot on a number line and shows spread and clusters but loses the original order.
concepts.example: Runs 0, 17, 21, 90 have range 90 and runs 67, 55, 18, 35 have range 49, so the second set is more consistent.

concepts.name: Median and outliers
concepts.description: Finding the median of sorted data with an odd or even number of values and recognising outliers and their pull on the mean.
concepts.idea: The median is the middle value, so a few very large or very small values cannot move it much.
concepts.rule: Sort the data; the median is the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even; an outlier is a value far from the rest.
concepts.example: The heights 118, 165, 170, 173, 175 have median 170 but mean 160.2, because 118 is an outlier.

concepts.name: Mean and median compared, zero and missing values
concepts.description: Comparing the mean and median, choosing the measure that represents the data, and treating a zero score differently from a missing value.
concepts.idea: An outlier pulls the mean towards itself, and only values that really belong to the data should be counted.
concepts.rule: No outlier: mean and median are close; high outlier: mean greater than median; low outlier: mean less than median; a missing value is not counted, a zero is.
concepts.example: 57, 13, 0, 84, -, 51, 27 has 6 values, not 7, because the player did not play one match.

concepts.name: Double bar (clustered column) graphs
concepts.description: Reading and drawing double bar graphs, choosing a scale, converting between values and bar lengths, and interpreting them in two steps.
concepts.idea: Putting two bars side by side for each category on one scale lets us compare groups directly.
concepts.rule: Bar length = value / scale unit; use different colours or patterns for the two groups; first identify what is given, then infer.
concepts.example: With 1 unit = 4 degrees C, a temperature of 26 degrees C is drawn as a bar 6.5 units long.

concepts.name: Reading data tables and finding stories in data
concepts.description: Reading tables of averages over ages and years, comparing groups, computing changes, and deciding which statements the data justify.
concepts.idea: Data tell a story only if we read exactly what they say, and averages do not describe every individual.
concepts.rule: Compare values by subtracting; a statement is justified only if the numbers in the table show it; one or two samples cannot be generalised.
concepts.example: Boys aged 5 in 1989 averaged 101.3 cm and in 2019 averaged 107.1 cm, an increase of 5.8 cm.
